1:
Twelve psalms carry Asaph's name, and whether he wrote them turns on a preposition. Clarke thinks he most probably did, being of high repute in David's day and named second to him as a composer. Calvin notes that the particle prefixed to the name admits two renderings, so it remains doubtful whether Asaph was the author or merely the man to whom David delivered them to be sung — though he judges authorship probable. Both report the same stylistic verdict: these are stiffer and more obscure than David's polished, flowing odes, their subject-matter melancholy and full of reprehension. Henry supposes Asaph was not only the chief musician but the penman. Delitzsch places the psalm rather than the man: it is the only Asaphic piece in the primary collection, set here because its call to hear echoes the psalm before. Calvin states the theme in advance: there have always been hypocrites who placed religion in a mere observance of ceremonies, and the psalm exposes the dishonour done to God by confounding ceremony with religion, showing that his worship is spiritual and consists of prayer and thanksgiving.

The three divine names at the head are handled as syntax and as ceremony. Ellicott reports that while the Authorised Version follows two ancient Greek translators in running the terms together, the Masoretic accents favour taking each as a separate appellative. The objection that this is stiff he grants and turns round: it is stiff on purpose, the poet introducing his vision of judgment in the style of a royal proclamation — and because the monarch is not an earthly one, its range is not territorial but runs from sunrise to sunset. Spurgeon reaches the same effect without the grammar: the august titles are stacked at the front as the names and dignities of monarchs are in royal decrees. Gill records the alternatives, God of gods and Judge of judges, and takes the title of Christ. Henry treats the verse as a court being called, all the earth summoned because at the last all nations shall be gathered to hear their doom.

Augustine goes elsewhere. Not any man nor any angel has spoken, he insists, but the God of gods — and he who called the world from sunrise to sunset is Christ, the Word made flesh, by whom all things were made, so that if any were made gods, by him they were made. He prefaces this with a demand that each reader set his conscience without deceit before his eyes, since God flatters no one.

On the shining out of Zion they agree in substance and differ in reach. Ellicott explains the epithet simply, Zion being the perfection of beauty because the temple stood there, and the shining a figure of divine manifestation drawn from dawn or lightning. Spurgeon presses the preposition: the majesty of God is most conspicuous among his elect but not confined to them, for the church is not a dark lantern but a candlestick, and he shines not only in Zion but out of her. Over the coming that follows, Ellicott marks the change of tense as the moment the drama opens; Wesley hears the worshippers themselves speaking, and observes that though he is our God he comes to execute judgment upon us; Gill rules out both the first coming, which was silent and unattended by fire, and the last. The summons to heaven and earth is read as evidence. Delitzsch raises the possibility that they are themselves ordered to gather the saints and rejects it, since gathering is no proper work of theirs, whereas existing from the beginning and destined to last for ever they are exactly suited to be witnesses. Ellicott adds the observation the others miss: Israel, politically so insignificant, must have been profoundly conscious of the issues involved in its religious character to demand a theatre so vast, an audience so august.
5:
Ellicott treats the summons of the saints as among the book's most important verses, because it defines a term used throughout. The saints are those in the covenant, ratified by sacrifice — from which he draws a conclusion governing the rest of the psalm. Since every sacrifice witnessed that the covenant existed, we are not to gather that outward sacrifice is annulled by the higher spirit taught here; it is subordinated to its place, and those censured thought more of the rites than of the duties the covenant enjoined. Wesley reads the clause as instruction: the words about covenant by sacrifice acquaint them with the end of sacrifices, appointed as signs and seals, and convict them of trusting the outward act while neglecting its life and soul. He takes the command as addressed to angels; Gill hears Christ speaking, extending the gathering through gospel ministers to the elect among the Gentiles.

The heavens answering draws Ellicott's warmest note: an exceedingly fine touch, the heavens acknowledging God's right to arraign. He restates it in modern terms: order in the physical world is evidence of an ordered moral government, and the obedience of the unconscious stars a challenge to man to submit consciously to the same will. Wesley expects something louder, God convincing the people by thunders and storms, not through priests or prophets but from heaven. When the speech begins, Delitzsch notes that the strengthened verb forms make God's desire for willing hearers as strong as his desire to speak, and that his self-designation reaches back to the opening words of the commandments. Spurgeon says the address is meant first for Israel but applies equally to the visible church in every age, declaring the futility of external worship where spiritual faith is absent. Henry finds the original contract restated — they had avouched him their God and he them his people — and adds that when God speaks his people should give ear; who will, if they do not?

What follows denies that the charge is ritual neglect. Ellicott renders it that God reproves them not on account of their sacrifices nor their burnt offerings, which are always before him, and observes that this part of the nation is judged not for neglect of ritual but for mistaken regard for it — the people separated, as usual in such visions, into two classes, the better reproved first. Henry puts it historically: the controversy was not that they had been wanting in the institutions, but that they took pride in them and hoped by their offerings to procure a dispensation for their lusts, as though sacrifice could excuse neglect of the law's weightier matters. Clarke agrees the fault was never in the offering but in the manner, then goes further than the others will: once the people began to trust the sacrifices without looking to the thing signified, it was time to put them away — his precedent being the brazen serpent, an ordinance of God's own appointment broken to pieces when divine honours began to be paid to it.

The argument from ownership goes briskly. Clarke turns it into questions: can you suppose you lay me under obligation by presenting part of my own property, or that I appointed such sacrifices for my own gratification? Wesley says it in one line: be not so foolish as to imagine you lay any obligation on me. Gill notes why the bullock is named, as the chief beast used in sacrifice. Ellicott stops over one phrase: what is rendered a thousand hills is literally mountains of a thousand, an expression for which there is no analogy. He thinks the Greek and Latin right to read oxen instead of a thousand, giving hills of oxen. Clarke closes by looking through the abolished rite to what it signified — a spiritual worship, and the sacrifice of the Lamb of God.
14:
The sacrifice God does want is named, and the readers take care that it not abolish the rest. Ellicott says gratitude and the performance of known duties are the ritual most pleasing to God, but insists the verse does not imply the cessation of outward rites, only the subordination of form to spirit. Wesley makes it a ranking: what is indispensably required is first thankfulness — which does not consist barely in verbal acknowledgments but proceeds from a heart deeply affected with God's mercies; the vows are the substantial promises that were the soul of their sacrifices. Gill points out that thanksgiving is itself a sacrifice, records the saying that in the days of the Messiah every sacrifice will cease except praise, and notes a rendering that gives confession instead. Clarke goes the other way and specifies the rite: the thank-offering was a bullock or ram without blemish, with unleavened cakes mingled with oil, wafers anointed with oil, and cakes of fine flour fried; the vow-offering a male from the flock. Having set them out he says what they were for: a system to show the sinfulness of sin and the purity of God, now ending in the thing it signified.

The call to prayer is treated briefly. Gill takes invocation to cover all religious worship and here to mean prayer in particular, offered in faith and fervency, especially under affliction. Wesley calls it a duty to be made conscience of, an acknowledgment of dependence, the deliverance promised carrying its own obligation.

Then the psalm turns, and the question is whether to new people or the same. Delitzsch is explicit that those addressed at the opening of the speech are not those addressed now, naming the accusation of the manifest sinners a distinct movement and correcting a scholar who ran them together. Ellicott agrees, describing a turn to a worse class — men undisguisedly wicked who shelter under the covenant name — and renders the challenge, how darest thou. Spurgeon draws the line through the commandments: the earlier rebuke went to neglecters of the first table, this one to breakers of the second, and if lack of heart spoiled the worship of the more decent, how much more do open violations corrupt the sacrifices of the wicked? Gill reads the division historically: the preceding verses concern godly Jews who believed in Christ and were still zealous of the law, these words the hypocrites among them.

Who is meant divides them further. Gill is specific: not openly profane sinners, but men under a profession of religion, teachers who sat in Moses's chair and said and did not. Clarke names them more bluntly, the bloodthirsty priests, proud Pharisees and ignorant scribes. Henry reports the same application, then widens it. The verse challenges those really profane but seemingly godly to show their title to the cloak of religion, when they use it only to conceal the impieties of their lives; if it points at teachers who declared God's statutes while hating Christ's instruction, it applies as well to any practiser of iniquity who professes piety, especially one who preaches it. It is possible, and too common, for men who declare God's statutes to live in disobedience to them, and for men who take his covenant in their mouths to keep in their hearts a covenant with sin; such men usurp an honour they have no title to, and a day is coming when they will be thrust out as intruders. Spurgeon presses the charge as accusations: you violate the moral law openly and are great sticklers for the ceremonial, counting up holy days while despising the weightier matters; a claim to be sons of Levi will not serve, since the wickedness itself puts a man out of the succession. Wesley reduces it to the question the verse asks: with what confidence dare you mention the grace that gave you the covenant?
17:
The indictment is read as a portrait of religious professionals. Gill takes the hated instruction to be correction by the very statutes they declared to others. On consenting with a thief he presses the identification hard: these men devoured widows' houses under pretence of long prayers, preferred a robber to Christ, and joined the thieves on the cross in reviling him. Clarke says only that rapine and adulterous divines were common in that generation. Ellicott works the verbs: consenting means having pleasure in, giving the mouth to evil is letting it loose, framing deceit is weaving — a figure common to all languages. He prefers lurkest to sittest, notes that the word behind slander means literally to give a thrust, and observes that where polygamy was practised mother's son marks a closer relation than brother. Gill reads the sitting concretely, in the chair of Moses or on the judgment seat.

The verse about God's silence draws the sharpest analysis. Ellicott states the mechanism: God's forbearance, meant to give room for repentance, is misconstrued, and men come to think the divine Being as indifferent to evil as themselves. He would render the next clause as that I was actually such a one, and objects to the word supplied in the last line, preferring thine offences. Wesley says it pastorally: the patience was misconstrued as approbation, so the sins will now be laid on the conscience. Clarke keeps it short: the eye was continually upon them, though the judgments were not poured out. Gill treats it as confirmation of a charge laid by one who saw every action.

The appeal that follows is heard as entreaty rather than sentence. Spurgeon reads the opening word as a plea, the Lord being loath to let even the most ungodly run on, and directs it at both classes — you who trust in ceremonies and you who live in vice, for both alike forget God. He defends the harshness of the threat: God uses no soft words or velvet metaphors, nor may his servants when they speak of the wrath to come. Delitzsch reads it the same way, taking those who forget God to comprehend both the decent, whose sanctity relies on outward works, and those who know better but give way to licentiousness; the accepted offering he defines as thanksgiving of the heart, not the sacrifice of that name. Clarke turns it into a warning with one exit: the iniquities are marked down to be exhibited, and none can deliver but the Christ they reject. Gill defines the consideration asked as repentance, a reconsideration of sin.

The last verse returns to the sacrifice named earlier, and its second half will not sit still. Clarke observes that the words are identical to those used before and should be read the same way, as sacrifice the thank-offering, and takes the ordering of one's way as disposing it, or making that one's custom. Ellicott agrees on the first clause, which sums up the psalm, then makes a division the others do not: this half addresses the sincere formalist, the next the openly wicked. That forces the second half to speak of amendment, and the received text will not give it — placeth his way is hardly intelligible — so he canvasses two emendations, one yielding him who walks uprightly, the other, which he prefers, him who has turned his way. Spurgeon takes the received wording as it stands and makes holy living a choice evidence of salvation, with the caution that the best ordering of a life cannot save, though the man who orders it shall have salvation. Not the lowing of bullocks bound to the altar, he says, but the songs of redeemed men are the music God's ear delights in — which is Wesley's point in one line: such a man, and not the man who loads the altar, gives God the honour he requires.
